glossary.definition: The derivative of the expression appearing inside an exponential, logarithm or trigonometric function.
The derivative evaluated at the input of the point of contact.

revision.body:
What stays when an exponential differentiates?

For \(y=ae^{u(x)}+b\), with a and b constant, use \(y'=au'(x)e^{u(x)}\).

What if the exponent decreases with x?

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}e^{-kx+c}=-ke^{-kx+c}\). For k positive, the derivative is negative.

What changes when a linear factor multiplies the exponential?

For \(y=u(x)e^{v(x)}\), use \(y'=(u'+uv')e^v\).

Quick worked example

Find the equation of the tangent to \(y=e^x\) at \(x=0\).

The point is \((0,e^0)=(0,1)\).

The derivative is \(e^x\), so the tangent gradient at zero is \(1\).

Use \(y-1=1(x-0)\), giving \(y=x+1\).
revision.checks:
• Only a constant added outside the exponential differentiates to zero. A constant inside the exponent remains.
  • A positive function can have a negative derivative. The sign of the derivative describes change, not height.
revision.examTip: Keep an exact exponential expression until the final requested approximation.

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
blocks.prompt:
A function is given by \(y=12 \ln{\left(2 x + 2 \right)} - 3\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

blocks.solution:
Set \(u=2 x + 2\). The derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(\frac{1}{2 x + 2}\) times the derivative of u.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{24}{2 x + 2}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{24}{2 x + 2}\).

blocks.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain

A function is given by \(y=- 7 x + 11 \ln{\left(8 x - 5 \right)}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: The linear term differentiates to its coefficient. Add the derivative of the logarithm obtained by the chain rule.
blocks.solution:
The derivative of the logarithm uses its input in the denominator, so \(11 \ln{\left(8 x - 5 \right)}\) contributes \(\frac{88}{8 x - 5}\). Add the derivative of the linear term.

examples.title: Read a value and a gradient on the logarithm
examples.question: Find the tangent to \(y=\ln x\) at \(x=1\).
solution: The domain is \(x>0\). At the chosen input, \(\ln 1=0\), giving \((1,0)\).
The derivative is \(\frac1x\), giving a slope of \(1\).

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its real domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=2 \ln{\left(3 x - 8 \right)} + 7\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2}{3 x - 8}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-9 + \frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=11 + \frac{6}{3 x - 8}\)
solution: Let \(u=3x-8\). The domain requires \(u>0\), so \(x>\frac83\). For \(y=2\ln u+7\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm du}=\frac2u\).
Multiply by \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=3\). Thus \(y^\prime=\frac6{3x-8}\), option A.

examples.title: Distinguish a domain argument from a slope argument
examples.question: For \(y=2\ln(7-3x)\), find its domain and gradient at \(x=2\).
solution: At \(x=2\), the denominator is \(1\), so the gradient is \(-6\).

examples.title: Keep the negative inner derivative of a logarithm
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=10 \ln{\left(1 - 2 x \right)} - 7\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{10}{1 - 2 x}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-9 - \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=11 - \frac{20}{1 - 2 x}\)
solution: Let \(u=1-2x\), so the domain requires \(x<\frac12\). The outer derivative is \(\frac{10}{u}\).
Multiply by the inner derivative \(-2\). This gives \(y^\prime=-\frac{20}{1-2x}\), option A.

examples.title: Use the addition rule before solving a gradient equation
examples.question: Find where \(y=2\ln x+x\) has gradient \(3\).
solution: Substitution gives slope \(2+1=3\) at an allowed input.

examples.title: Differentiate a logarithm on its correct domain
examples.question:
A function is given by \(y=- 8 x + 11 \ln{\left(9 x - 7 \right)}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-8 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-8 + \frac{11}{9 x - 7}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-17 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=3 + \frac{99}{9 x - 7}\)
solution: The derivative of the logarithm uses its input in the denominator, so \(11 \ln{\left(9 x - 7 \right)}\) contributes \(\frac{99}{9 x - 7}\). Add the derivative of the linear term.

revision.body:
Why does the logarithmic argument matter?

On \(u(x)>0\), the derivative of \(\ln(u(x))\) is \(\frac{u'(x)}{u(x)}\).

What if the inner slope is negative?

For \(u=a-bx\) with \(b>0\), use \(x<\frac ab\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\ln(a-bx)=-\frac{b}{a-bx}\).

How do you differentiate a logarithm plus a linear term?

On \(ax+b>0\),\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\bigl(c\ln(ax+b)+dx\bigr)=\frac{ca}{ax+b}+d\).

Quick worked example

Find the tangent to \(y=\ln x\) at \(x=1\).

The domain is \(x>0\). At the chosen input, \(\ln 1=0\), giving \((1,0)\).

The derivative is \(\frac1x\), giving a slope of \(1\).

The tangent equation is \(y=x-1\).
revision.checks:
• The derivative expression may exist for some inputs where the original logarithm is undefined.
  • The gradient denominator is positive where the logarithm is defined. Its sign comes from the numerator.
revision.examTip: Before using the derivative at a specific point, check that the logarithmic argument there is positive.

examples.title: Connect the sine curve to its slope
examples.question: Find the gradient of \(y=\sin x\) at \(x=\frac\pi2\).
solution: On either side of \(\frac\pi2\), the slope changes from positive to negative, so this point is a local maximum.

examples.title: Simplify the radian angle after differentiating
examples.question:
The curve is \(y=9 \sin{\left(8 x + \frac{\pi}{5} \right)} + 10\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact gradient when \(x=\frac{\pi}{60}\).
solution: At \(x=\frac\pi{60}\), the angle is \(\frac{8\pi}{60}+\frac{\pi}{5}=\frac\pi3\), so the gradient is \(72\cdot\frac12=36\).

examples.title: Use both signs when differentiating cosine
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of \(y=3\cos(\pi-2x)\) at \(x=\frac\pi4\).
solution: The inner derivative is \(-2\). The cosine derivative includes another minus sign.
At \(x=\frac\pi4\), the angle is \(\frac\pi2\) and the slope is \(6\).

examples.title: Use the negative sine and the exact angle
examples.question:
The curve is \(y=10 \cos{\left(5 x + \frac{2 \pi}{7} \right)} - 7\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact gradient when \(x=\frac{\pi}{105}\).
solution: The derivative is \(-50\sin(5x+\frac{2\pi}{7})\). The sign comes from differentiating cosine.
At \(x=\frac{\pi}{105}\), the angle is \(\frac{\pi}{21}+\frac{6\pi}{21}=\frac\pi3\). The gradient is \(-50\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=-25\sqrt3\).

extraPractice.title: Match a trigonometric gradient to its inner factor
extraPractice.prompt: For \(y=\sin(kx)\) with \(k>0\), the gradient at \(x=0\) is 5. Find k.
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate before substituting the zero angle.
extraPractice.solution: \(y'=k\cos(kx)\). At zero, \(y'=k\). Therefore \(k=5\).

revision.body:
What changes from sine to cosine?

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\sin u(x)=u'(x)\cos u(x)\) for radian angles.

Where does the minus sign come from?

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\cos u(x)=-u'(x)\sin u(x)\).

How does tangent differentiate?

\(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\tan u(x)=u'(x)\sec^2u(x)\) where \(\cos u(x)\ne0\).

Quick worked example

Find the gradient of \(y=\sin x\) at \(x=\frac\pi2\).

The derivative is \(\cos x\) in radians.

The value \(\cos\frac\pi2=0\) gives a horizontal tangent.

On either side of \(\frac\pi2\), the slope changes from positive to negative, so this point is a local maximum.
revision.checks:
• If the argument is 4x, the derivative includes a factor of 4.
  • An inner derivative that is negative can cancel the outer negative sign.

sections.title: How does a positive factor help at a stationary point?
sections.label: Positive factor

blocks.html: Since \(e^x>0\) everywhere, \(e^x g(x)=0\) exactly when \(g(x)=0\).

figure.alt: The graph decreases until x = −1, where it has a horizontal tangent, then increases.
figure.caption: The graph decreases until x = −1, where it has a horizontal tangent, then increases.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Use the product rule and factor out the exponential.
  2. Find zeros of the remaining factor only.
  3. Prove the nature from the remaining factor's sign or from the second derivative.

blocks.title: Isolate the factor that can be zero
blocks.prompt: Find the stationary x-coordinate of \(y=(x-2)e^{2x}\).
blocks.hint: Factor out the positive exponential after differentiating. Solve the remaining bracket.

retry.feedback: Two is a zero of the original function. Solve the derivative equation to find a stationary input.

blocks.html: An exponential can approach zero, but it is strictly positive at every finite input.

blocks.title: Find a stationary point in an exponential product
blocks.prompt:
The function is \(y=\left(11 x - 55\right) e^{4 x - 20} - 10\).

Find the x-coordinate of the stationary point.
blocks.hint: Set the derivative to zero and use the fact that the exponential factor is positive.
blocks.solution:
An exponential cannot be zero. Set the remaining bracket equal to zero.

Answer: \(\frac{19}{4}\).

retry.feedback: The positive exponential is never a root. Solve only the remaining factor.

sections.intro: A factored derivative can make the stationary equation simpler. If a factor is always positive, it cannot contribute a zero, but it preserves the sign of the remaining factor.

sections.title: Which expressions give the point and gradient?
sections.label: Log tangent

blocks.html: When \(ax+b=1\), \(\ln(ax+b)=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\ln(ax+b)=a\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Check the input is in the logarithm's domain.
  2. Calculate the point and gradient from the two different formulas.
  3. Write the line through the point and verify it there.

blocks.title: Use a negative logarithmic slope
blocks.prompt: Find the equation of the tangent to \(y=\ln(5-2x)\) at \(x=2\).
blocks.hint: At this input the argument is 1. Its derivative has a negative sign.

retry.feedback: The line should fall with slope −2. Keep that sign in the line equation.

blocks.html: Knowing a derivative value gives the gradient only. Use the original curve for the point.

blocks.title: Find a tangent to a logarithmic curve
blocks.prompt:
Consider \(y=\ln{\left(8 x + 4 \right)}\), on the domain \(8 x + 4>0\).

Find the equation of the tangent at \(x=- \frac{3}{8}\).
blocks.hint: Use the original curve for the point and the derivative for the slope, then write the point–slope equation.
blocks.solution:
The point is \((- \frac{3}{8},0)\). The gradient is \(8\).

Use \(y-y_0=m(x-x_0)\).

Answer: \(y=8 x + 3\).

sections.intro: A logarithmic curve gives the height, and its derivative gives the slope. Choosing an input where the argument is 1 can simplify both.

sections.title: How do you use the interval when solving a derivative equation?
sections.label: Trig stationary

blocks.html: At a stationary input for \(y=\sin(kx)\) with \(k\ne0\), solve \(\cos(kx)=0\) within the corresponding angle interval.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Translate the x interval into one for the full angle.
  2. Find all solutions within that angle interval.
  3. Convert to x-coordinates and justify the nature when asked.

blocks.title: Give both stationary x-values
blocks.prompt: Find the stationary x-values of \(y=\cos(3x)\) for \(0<x<\pi\).
blocks.hint: In the angle interval from zero to 3π, list every interior angle at which sine is zero.
blocks.solution:
\(y'=-3\sin(3x)\). Within \(0<3x<3\pi\), the sine is zero at \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\).

Divide by 3 to obtain \(x=\frac\pi3\) or \(x=\frac{2\pi}3\).

retry.feedback: There is a second interior zero at angle 2π. Convert it back to x as well.

blocks.html: A correct trigonometric angle can be an incorrect x-coordinate if you forget the final conversion.

blocks.title: Find a turn of a trigonometric curve on a restricted interval
blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(2 x \right)} - 8\) for \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact x-coordinate of the stationary point.
blocks.hint: Rewrite the interval in terms of the bracketed angle before solving the trigonometric equation.
blocks.solution:
Set \(- 4 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\) to zero to obtain equal sine and cosine. In the stated interval this gives \(kx=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

Answer: \(\frac{\pi}{8}\).

retry.feedback: The angle solving the trigonometric equation is kx. Convert it back to an x-coordinate.

blocks.html: For a stationary point state its exact coordinates and justify its nature with a derivative test.

sections.intro: If the angle is a multiple of x, first convert the whole restriction into an interval for the angle. Convert back after solving.

examples.title: Locate and classify the turn without logarithms
examples.question: Find and classify the stationary point of \(y=xe^x\).
solution: The sign changes from negative to positive through −1. The point \((-1,-e^{-1})\) is a local minimum.

examples.title: Find a zero of the non-exponential factor
examples.question:
The function is \(y=\left(11 x - 66\right) e^{4 x - 24} + 4\).

Find the x-coordinate of the stationary point.
solution: Factor to get \(y^\prime=11(4x-23)e^{4x-24}\). The exponential is positive, so the derivative vanishes only when \(4x-23=0\).

examples.title: Construct the tangent with a simple logarithmic point
examples.question: Find the tangent to \(y=\ln(2x+1)+3\) at \(x=0\).
solution: The logarithm's argument is \(1\) and the height is \(3\), giving \((0,3)\).

examples.title: Get the point and slope of a logarithmic tangent
examples.question:
Consider \(y=9 \ln{\left(2 x + 6 \right)} + 7\), on the domain \(2 x + 6>0\).

Find the equation of the tangent at \(x=- \frac{5}{2}\).
solution: At \(x=-\frac52\), the logarithm argument equals \(1\), so the original curve gives the point \((-\frac52,7)\).
The derivative is \(\frac{18}{2x+6}\). Its value is \(18\) at the point.

examples.title: Keep both stationary points in the interval
examples.question: Find and classify the stationary points of \(y=\sin(2x)\) for \(0<x<\pi\).
solution: \(y''=-4\sin(2x)\) is negative at the first input, giving maximum \(1\), and positive at the second, giving minimum \(-1\).

examples.title: Solve the stationary condition in the correct angle interval
examples.question:
The curve is \(y=13 \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 13 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\) for \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{4}\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact x-coordinate of the stationary point.
solution: Differentiate to get \(y^\prime=52\cos(4x)-52\sin(4x)\). Set this to zero, giving \(\cos(4x)=\sin(4x)\).
Let \(\theta=4x\). Then \(0<\theta<\pi\). Within this interval the equality holds only at \(\theta=\frac\pi4\).

extraPractice.title: Find a stationary point in an exponential product
extraPractice.prompt:
The function is \(y=\left(6 x - 24\right) e^{5 x - 20} - 6\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate the linear factor and exponential factor separately. Factor out the exponential from the sum.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the product rule on the linear and exponential factors, then factor out the always-positive \(e^{5 x - 20}\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6 \left(5 x - 19\right) e^{5 x - 20}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=6 \left(5 x - 19\right) e^{5 x - 20}\).

retry.feedback: The positive exponential is never a root. Solve only the remaining factor.

Find the x-coordinate of the stationary point.
extraPractice.hint: Set the derivative to zero and use the fact that the exponential factor is positive.
extraPractice.solution:
An exponential cannot be zero. Set the remaining bracket equal to zero.

Answer: \(\frac{8}{3}\).

retry.feedback: The positive exponential is never a root. Solve only the remaining factor.

extraPractice.title: Find a tangent to a logarithmic curve
extraPractice.prompt:
Consider \(y=2 \ln{\left(3 x - 5 \right)} + 6\), on the domain \(3 x - 5>0\).

Find the exact gradient when \(x=2\).
extraPractice.hint: Check that the logarithm argument is positive at the stated input. Use its derivative in the numerator.
extraPractice.solution:
Evaluate \(\frac{6}{3 x - 5}\) at the stated input.

Answer: \(6\).

retry.feedback: A line needs the gradient and the point. Substituting into the derivative alone does not find the point.

extraPractice.title: Find a tangent to a logarithmic curve
extraPractice.prompt:
Consider \(y=6 \ln{\left(6 x \right)} - 3\), on the domain \(6 x>0\).

Find the equation of the tangent at \(x=\frac{1}{6}\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the original curve for the point and the derivative for the slope, then write the point–slope equation.
extraPractice.solution:
The point is \((\frac{1}{6},-3)\). The gradient is \(36\).

Use \(y-y_0=m(x-x_0)\).

Answer: \(y=36 x - 9\).

extraPractice.title: Find a turn of a trigonometric curve on a restricted interval
extraPractice.prompt:
The curve is \(y=8 \sin{\left(6 x \right)} + 8 \cos{\left(6 x \right)} - 10\) for \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{6}\). Angles are in radians.

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate both trigonometric terms. Keep the multiplier from the shared argument.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both trigonometric terms and preserve the inner factor.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- 48 \sin{\left(6 x \right)} + 48 \cos{\left(6 x \right)}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- 48 \sin{\left(6 x \right)} + 48 \cos{\left(6 x \right)}\).

retry.feedback: The angle solving the trigonometric equation is kx. Convert it back to an x-coordinate.

extraPractice.title: Choose the local maximum from the second derivative
extraPractice.prompt: For \(y=2\cos(2x)\) on \(0<x<2\pi\), find the x-coordinate of its local maximum.
extraPractice.hint: Find the zeros of sin(2x) inside the interval. Then compare the signs of y″ there.
extraPractice.solution:
\(y'=-4\sin(2x)\). The stationary inputs are \(\frac\pi2\), \(\pi\) and \(\frac{3\pi}2\).

\(y''=-8\cos(2x)\) is negative only at \(x=\pi\), so that input gives the local maximum.

retry.feedback: At x = π/2, the second derivative is positive. Look for its negative value.

revision.body:
How does a positive factor help at a stationary point?

Since \(e^x>0\) everywhere, \(e^x g(x)=0\) exactly when \(g(x)=0\).

Which expressions give the point and gradient?

When \(ax+b=1\), \(\ln(ax+b)=0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\ln(ax+b)=a\).

How do you use the interval when solving a derivative equation?

At a stationary input for \(y=\sin(kx)\) with \(k\ne0\), solve \(\cos(kx)=0\) within the corresponding angle interval.

Quick worked example

Find and classify the stationary point of \(y=xe^x\).

\(y'=e^x+xe^x=e^x(x+1)\).

Because \(e^x>0\), the only zero is at \(x=-1\).

The sign changes from negative to positive through −1. The point \((-1,-e^{-1})\) is a local minimum.

previousChecks.title: Find a turn of a trigonometric curve on a restricted interval
previousChecks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=5 \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\) for \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{4}\). Angles are in radians.

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
previousChecks.hint: Differentiate both trigonometric terms. Keep the multiplier from the shared argument.
previousChecks.solution:
Differentiate both trigonometric terms and preserve the inner factor.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- 20 \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 20 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- 20 \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + 20 \cos{\left(4 x \right)}\).

retry.feedback: The angle solving the trigonometric equation is kx. Convert it back to an x-coordinate.

previousChecks.title: Find a turn of a trigonometric curve on a restricted interval
previousChecks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=10 \sin{\left(9 x \right)} + 10 \cos{\left(9 x \right)} + 2\) for \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{9}\). Angles are in radians.

Find the exact x-coordinate of the stationary point.
previousChecks.hint: Rewrite the interval in terms of the bracketed angle before solving the trigonometric equation.
previousChecks.solution:
Set \(- 90 \sin{\left(9 x \right)} + 90 \cos{\left(9 x \right)}\) to zero to obtain equal sine and cosine. In the stated interval this gives \(kx=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

Answer: \(\frac{\pi}{36}\).
